One might object that this statement, the one before it, and the earlier examples we cited of the intellect forming universals from particulars—as in the case of an eclipse—occur in Ibn Sīnā’s discussion of divine matters, or metaphysics, and therefore do not apply to the material world. Our answer is twofold. First, Ibn Sīnā uses ideas of this kind in that context because he treats them as general principles already accepted in the particular sciences, such as natural science and mathematics. He then uses them as grounds for his views in “divine science.” Second, we do not separate a philosopher’s ideas in metaphysics from his ideas in other fields. All of them come from a single source: the real world reflected in his thought in one form or another. His metaphysical ideas are simply one form of that reflection. They are particular echoes of the way he relates to the real world and of his particular position in society.↩︎

The editor of this edition of Pointers and Reminders prints the phrase as: “...its essence, which is not [from] existence.” In a footnote he says that three manuscripts read: “...its essence, which is not existence.” We do not know why the editor, Sulaymān Dunyā, added the word “from” when all three manuscripts omit it. We think the reading found in those three manuscripts, without “from,” is more likely to be Ibn Sīnā’s original wording, because it means that essence is different from existence and therefore cannot be its cause.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā often describes the individuating features of a particular thing as “accidents” or “concomitants” that are foreign to its essence—meaning its substance and true nature. We should not take this to mean that he imagines the substance of a thing as a spiritual substance to which matter is attached only accidentally or by chance. That idea is far from his thought. Although he calls these material individuating features “accidents” or “concomitants,” he still regards them as necessarily bound up with the existence of things and impossible to separate from them. We will clarify this point further when we study the theory of form and matter in Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy.↩︎

Aristotle sees the relation of matter to form as similar to the relation of the individual to the universal that includes it and other individuals. Form, in other words, is the concept or essence in relation to matter. Callias and Socrates, Aristotle’s example, are the same in species but differ from one another in their matter (Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1034a 5 ff.). Ibn Sīnā, by contrast, treats matter as the underlying “subject” in relation to form, and this subject is a substance. “Subject” and “substance” are not the same as essence. See The Salvation, p. 200; and al-Shahrastānī, Religions and Sects, vol. 2, p. 74. We will explain this point in detail in the discussion that follows.↩︎

In defining the subject of natural science, Ibn Sīnā says that it is “existing bodies insofar as they undergo change and insofar as they are described by different kinds of motion and rest” (The Salvation, p. 98).↩︎

Aristotle’s dualism of matter and form appears in two ways. First, he treats matter as merely receptive and passive, while form alone is active and acts upon matter. He does not recognize the dialectical unity of mutual influence between them in the way Ibn Sīnā does. See Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1029a 19. Second, matter itself has a double character in Aristotle’s view. Matter is potentiality in relation to form, while form is the actual realization of that potentiality. Matter is therefore pure possibility on one side, and an actual reality realized through form on the other. In this sense it becomes relative: a thing is matter—that is, existence—from one point of view, and form—that is, concept—from another. Matter in itself is therefore not treated as something definite in relation to form. See Aristotle, same source, 7, 1041a–b 5–6. We will see in the course of the discussion how Ibn Sīnā overcame this problem partly, if not completely.↩︎

In ancient and then medieval philosophy, the term “divine science” meant philosophy of existence in its broadest sense—universal being as a whole. It was the main branch of ancient philosophy, which is why Aristotle called it “first philosophy.” Philosophy at that time included all the sciences and was even called “the science of sciences.” Sciences that dealt with particular kinds of existence, such as natural science, mathematics, and social science, were called particular sciences. For this reason, when Ibn Sīnā speaks of “divine science” in this older sense, we treat him as speaking about philosophy, and we treat the principles of that science as the principles of philosophy itself.↩︎

Alongside the many examples already mentioned and others that will appear later, we can give one concrete example here. It occurs in The Salvation (pp. 236–237) in the proof of the Necessary Existent, within the “divine” section of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy. In arguing that “there must be something that necessarily exists,” Ibn Sīnā uses a proof by division in the Platonic manner. When his divisions of possible existence reach the possibility of something coming into being and then ceasing to exist immediately, with no interval of time—in other words, coming to be and passing away at the same instant—he says this is impossible “because instants do not follow one another [as discrete units], and for numerically distinct individuals to come into existence one after another without the continuity found in something like motion would require instants [times] to follow one another, and natural science has already shown this to be impossible....” Ibn Sīnā is therefore using a law of natural science as part of a proof in “divine science.” This is a concrete example of how he relies on theoretical generalizations drawn from the study of nature in arguments concerning the metaphysical world.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā does not picture the “first mover” as motionless in the way Aristotle does. He speaks clearly and explicitly on this point: “A mover implies something moved. But this implication does not mean that the moved thing must be something other than the mover, or that it must be the mover itself. (...) We therefore did not rule out the possibility of conceiving something that moves itself until a proof establishes that this is impossible. The mere concepts of mover and moved do not themselves rule it out. A moved thing requires something from which its motion comes, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself; and a mover requires something moved by it, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself....” The Salvation, p. 244.↩︎

Elsewhere in Pointers and Reminders (vol. 3, pp. 88–89), Ibn Sīnā also explains that terms such as “acted,” “made,” and “brought into existence” are used when something was first non-existent and then comes into existence after non-existence because of some cause. We then call it an effect, or something produced. An eternal existent, therefore, is not called an effect because, as he says in the passage quoted above, “non-existence did not precede it.” This confirms that Ibn Sīnā deliberately rejects the relation of acting, agency, and being acted upon between the first cause and its effect, the world, because this effect is as eternal as its cause.↩︎
